Feature: A Lost Box Restored My Faith In Zelda's Staying Power

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1042 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nintendolife

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A few weeks ago, my brother sent me a photo with zero context.
  • It took me a second to dust off the cobwebs in that corner of my mind, but once I did, I recognised the box as the promotional material Nintendo sent me back in 1998 to celebrate the original release of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.
  • Industry observers note that I asked my bro what was inside the box and a few moments later he replied with another picture.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A few weeks ago, my brother sent me a photo with zero context. He was at our parents’ house, helping them pack up for a cross-country move, when he found something unusual: a heavy metal box with a latch.

It took me a second to dust off the cobwebs in that corner of my mind, but once I did, I recognised the box as the promotional material Nintendo sent me back in 1998 to celebrate the original release of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

Industry observers note that I asked my bro what was inside the box and a few moments later he replied with another picture. The box was empty.

Sources indicate that I can’t think of anything more depressing than an empty treasure chest. All the anticipation leading to… crushing disappointment. Anyone who ever slogged through the Phoenix Cave in Final Fantasy VI knows the feeling.

Recent findings suggest that this chest originally housed a pre-launch, gold N64 cart of Ocarina of Time. It was Nintendo’s not-so-subtle message that this game was a treasure. A bit on the nose, but the zeitgeist of an entire generation of gamers has certainly proven them right. OoT is a treasure.

In a recent development, in this case, I can at least take solace knowing that I'm the one who emptied the chest and thoroughly enjoyed its golden treasure. The empty box is evidence of that.

My brother’s timing was impeccable — bordering on eerie — unearthing the box less than a week before the Switch 2 remake introduced.

Like many of you, my son (let's call him Tim) and I were eagerly awaiting the OoT remake. He hadn’t played the original, but is an avid Zelda fan, particularly the modern titles. I knew I’d love the Remake, but I was a bit nervous that he would have a different reaction. He’s a member of this Breath of the Wild, open-world generation, after all. Would the old-school Zelda formula appeal to his generation, or would it die with mine?

As they say, sometimes one man’s treasure is another man’s trash.

Recent findings suggest that my love for Zelda, and desire to pass it down to my son, parallels the experience my father had with his four boys. Dad loved to work with his hands and my brothers and I were always enlisted in projects: everything from clearing the land, felling trees, reroofing the house, building an addition, repainting, and working on a long series of rundown cars. He made sure we received hands-on working experience.

In a recent development, right around the time I received the Zelda Treasure Chest, my dad began restoring classic Ford Mustangs in his garage. I had already moved out, but my youngest brother ( the one who found the chest) was there to be Dad’s understudy. Together they restored two beautiful Mustangs, allowing my dad to share his love for mechanical craft and manual labour.

Sharing an old classic is one thing, but actually passing down a passion depends on how well the original holds up to modern sensibilities.

A restored car regains its iconic look, but it will also retain the old feel, complete with stiff brakes and crank windows. After all, restoring something doesn’t place it in a state opposite to its nature. A 1967 Mustang GT Fastback is a 1967 Mustang GT Fastback only if it looks, sounds, and feels like a 1967 Mustang GT Fastback, for better or worse.

In a recent development, media remakes and remasters are often criticised for following this type of approach. Shot-for-shot remakes come across as unnecessary cash grabs (looking at you Disney) while complete reimaginings seem to either spectacularly succeed (Dune, Casino Royale, Metroid Zero Mission) or fail (Planet of the Apes 2001, Secret of Mana, Quantum Leap).

Industry observers note that like my old man, Nintendo’s philosophy seems closer to restoration than reimagining. Star Fox and Super Mario RPG are recent examples, with the slightly more ambitious Link’s Awakening preceding them by a few years. There are many others.

It has been revealed that in each case, the spirit of the original is preserved while a few quality-of-life improvements are added. And of course, each old classic receives a new coat of paint.

By taking this approach, Nintendo has been careful to avoid the pitfalls that so many media companies encounter when updating beloved products. Their roster of remakes have largely avoided any 'Han shot first' controversies. Thank goodness.

A philosophy of preserving the original’s frame, while souping up the engine, allows old and new players to enjoy the gaming experience without fighting retro clunkiness.

So, what does Tim think of Ocarina of Time?

It has been revealed that he loves it, of course! And it’s been immensely satisfying to see him enjoy it. Confirmation bias can be a wonderful thing.

The wife and I have a ritual of playing Zelda games together, so we’re playing it in short, infrequent bursts. I’m not complaining, as it’s allowed me to savour the experience. Tim, on the other hand, is powering through it at a much faster pace. He also spectates while my wife and I play. We always aim for a 100% run, so Tim takes notes on all of the heart pieces and bag upgrades he missed.

I’m just excited to see my son enjoying a game I grew up with. My dad passed on his love for mechanical craft to his boys, and I’m sharing my passion for sidequests with mine.

Recent findings suggest that it’s been a good month. It began with a nostalgic relic and a bit of disappointment (grr, I still can’t find that gold cart), but also included a timeless masterpiece that’s been successfully passed to the next generation.

Industry observers note that 30 years ago my dad shared the muscle cars from his youth. This year I got to share a classic Zelda adventure from mine.

I wonder what treasure my boy will pass on to his kids in 30 years' time.

Have you successfully passed a favourite game down to the next generation? Was it the original, or a remake that added modern improvements? Share your stories in the comments below.

In a recent development, players who abused World of Warcraft: Forever's Blackmaw Hold unintended gold farm, which allowed a small minority of players to hoard thousands of gold in a few days, have drawn the ire of WoW publisher, Blizzard. Suspensions have been issued, trade locks have been put on accounts, and ill-gotten gold is being seized.

For those unaware, the World of Warcraft: Forever community was greatly alarmed by this gold farm, which had players clear the same non-elite enemies from the new late game dungeon, Blackmaw Hold. By rapidly clearing select mobs with area-of-effect damage, players would loot upwards of 100 raw gold an hour. This exploit, clearly not intentional, was nonetheless farmed until Blizzard hotfixed it earlier in the week.

In a recent development, there was much speculation on what would happen to those who participated in this exploit. That speculation would come to an end late last night with an official statement from the World of Warcraft: Forever development team.

"As players continue their journey into WoW Forever’s higher-level content, we are closely monitoring the game economy to ensure that gold sources and costs are well balanced," the statement reads. "Finding efficient farming spots has always been part of the game, and is how most players have earned their epic mounts since 2004. When a single location proves so lucrative that it overshadows all other sources, we generally adjust it to bring it in line with the rest.".

Industry observers note that it goes on to explain the nature of the bug that made this gold farm possible, before reassuring those who may have accidentally benefited from some extra cash from their regular runs of Blackmaw Hold they have nothing to worry about. The same cannot be said for those who took advantage of the situation.

Industry observers note that "Players who simply ran Blackmaw Hold a few times and benefited organically from the extra loot did nothing wrong, and no one should worry that they’re putting their account at risk if they accidentally benefit from a bug," it continues. "But there were a couple hundred players worldwide who recognized that this was unintended and spent significant time exclusively farming that group of enemies.

"Yesterday, we put an economy lock on their accounts to prevent broader impact to the game economy while we investigated the extent of the exploitative gains, including gold earned by vendoring bugged drops. Today, we are in the process of removing all such gold earned, as well as applying account suspensions to significant abusers.".

The post concludes by thanking players for their feedback on the matter, and a final warning: "As always, we advise all players to refrain from abusing game mechanics that are clearly unintended. We will continue to take action against intentional abuse.".

This decision certainly sets the precedent moving forward with World of Warcraft: Forever that such exploits won't be tolerated, and rolling back the wealth of those who made out of Blackmaw Hold like bandits is a good measure that should prevent continuous damage.

Inevitably the exploit would have had some impact, specifically in those days prior to trading blocks being put in place. While the gold on the exploiter's accounts may be removed, any purchases they made on the in-game auction house will have affected others through buying and selling goods with ample funds.

Recent findings suggest that those who were suspended temporarily will be able to regain access to the game by the time the first wave of raids come out in December, so it very much feels like a firm slap on the wrist in that regard. Even so, given the establishment of punishments for such behavior, one can only wonder if future events will come with harsher penalties.

Industry observers note that world of Warcraft: Forever, despite this small economic roadbump, is proving exceptionally popular for Blizzard. It's already broken records for the series, and has impressed players so far with its revamping of the classic MMO.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GTA 6 has been censored to a fairly large extent in Japan, where the country's strict ratings system often sees nudity, sexual content, and graphic violence be toned down or removed entirely in video games.

To be clear, GTA 6 has been given Japan's highest 18+ age rating — but it's still had to make changes in order to ensure its release in the region.

For starters, Rockstar's latest is packed with full-on nudity — to a degree never before seen in a mainstream release — but in Japan, it's apparently impossible to remove the underwear of main characters Jason and Lucia, even when they're taking a shower.

The same is true of NPCs — everyone's always wearing at least one layer to cover up their privates.

Recent findings suggest that needless to say, the game's numerous sex scenes have also been censored. Again, it's a case of keeping clothes on — but some specific scenes have actually been cut completely.

Violence is next on the list. GTA 6 obviously features a lot of bloodshed but it's also rather gory, with accurate depictions of dismemberment and lethal physical trauma. It can all come across as particularly gruesome given how realistic the game looks.

Recent findings suggest that in Japan, it seems as though most of this stuff is scaled back. There's less blood spray in general, and spilled blood doesn't stay in place very long.

It's a little unclear just how far this censorship of violence goes, but it's not uncommon for Japan to remove things like dismemberment — especially if a game's got a grounded setting.

Industry observers note that for what it's worth, GTA 6 does have several settings that let you change the amount of blood and gore that's on display. I assume that in Japan, these settings are applied at a censored standard by default.

Interestingly, though, drug use seemingly hasn't been touched. Japan's got very strict anti-drug laws, but illegal goods are still totally usable in GTA 6.

Recent findings suggest that did you see this censorship coming? Try not to go on a blood-soaked rampage in the comments section below.

Learn how to get a mask in GTA 6 to stay anonymous when committing a crime

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (607 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gamesradar

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that if you want to be a better criminal in Leonida, you're going to need to learn how to get a mask in GTA 6.
  • You can buy a mask in GTA 6 from any of the gun stores.
  • Sources indicate that to wear a mask in GTA 6, you need to make sure that it's with you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that if you want to be a better criminal in Leonida, you're going to need to learn how to get a mask in GTA 6. Despite Rockstar making appearance a key factor in the latest Wanted system, the game isn't super clear on the steps you can take to hide your identity – particularly as you're progressing through Chapter 1 of the GTA 6 missions list. Thankfully, I'm here to help you understand how to get neckwear in GTA 6, how to equip masks, and how to change them for new ones.

You can buy a mask in GTA 6 from any of the gun stores. Chuck's Tackle & Shot in Key Lento sells them (look at the central stand with the alligator head atop of it) from the beginning of the game, but you can head to any Ammu-Nation retailer to find more. Open up the GTA 6 Index, head into the weapons tab, and you'll be able to find all the relevant shops on your map. When you begin exploring Vice City and Vice Beach, you'll also find thrift stores that sell novelty masks, and high-end retailers which sell very fancy (and expensive) coverings that can be worn as well.

Sources indicate that to wear a mask in GTA 6, you need to make sure that it's with you. You can add neckwear items to your loadout by visiting the wardrobe in your residences. Scroll to the accessories tab and that's where you'll find the Masks option, which separates them by brand. If you want options while you're on the road, you can also store some in the trunk of your personal vehicle in GTA 6 by highlighting it and pressing Square/X.

With a mask in your loadout, wearing it is as simple as holding L1/LB to open your loadout. Press R1/RB to scroll to the items menu, and then select Mask from the neckwear slot located at twelve-o'clock in the wheel. Press A to put it on, press A to remove it. Easy enough, and vital if you want to lose some of your Appearance Heat after robbing a store with CCTV equipment.

While hovering over the neckwear slot of your loadout, you can also press up and down to change the wear style of your mask in GTA 6. The first will see the mask conceal your face, which will draw panicked reactions from shop clerks, while the second will let you fashion the mask more appropriately.
